{{Short description|Imaging technique used in seismology}}
[[File:LLSVP.gif|thumb|381x381px|Animation showing [[Large low-shear-velocity provinces|LLSVPs]] as inferred using '''seismic tomography'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Cottaar |last2=Lekic |date=2016 |title=Morphology of lower mantle structures |journal=[[Geophysical Journal International]] |volume=207 |issue=2 |pages=1122–1136 |bibcode=2016GeoJI.207.1122C |doi=10.1093/gji/ggw324 |doi-access=free}}</ref>]]

'''Seismic tomography''' or '''seismotomography''' is a technique for imaging the subsurface of the Earth using [[seismic wave]]s.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Nolet |first=G. |title=Seismic Tomography |date=1987-01-01 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-90-277-2583-7 |editor-last=Nolet |editor-first=Guust |series=Seismology and Exploration Geophysics |pages=1–23 |language=en |chapter=Seismic wave propagation and seismic tomography |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-3899-1_1}}</ref> The properties of seismic waves are modified by the material through which they travel. By comparing the differences in seismic waves recorded at different locations, it is possible to create a model of the subsurface structure. Most commonly, these seismic waves are generated by [[earthquake]]s or [[Seismic source|man-made sources]] such as explosions. Different types of waves, including [[P wave|P]], [[S wave|S]], [[Rayleigh wave|Rayleigh]], and [[Love wave|Love]] waves can be used for tomographic images, though each comes with their own benefits and downsides and are used depending on the geologic setting, [[seismometer]] coverage, distance from nearby earthquakes, and required resolution. The model created by tomographic imaging is almost always a [[Seismic velocity structure|seismic velocity model]], and features within this model may be interpreted as structural, thermal, or compositional variations. [[Geologist|Geoscientists]] apply seismic tomography to a wide variety of settings in which the subsurface structure is of interest, ranging in scale from [[Internal structure of Earth|whole-Earth structure]] to the upper few meters below the surface.

== Theory ==
[[Tomography]] is solved as an [[inverse problem]]. Seismic data are compared to an initial Earth model and the [[Scientific modelling|model]] is modified until the best possible fit between the model predictions and observed data is found. Seismic waves would travel in straight lines if Earth was of uniform composition, but [[Structural geology|structural]], chemical, and thermal variations affect the properties of seismic waves, most importantly their [[velocity]], leading to the reflection and refraction of these waves. The location and magnitude of variations in the subsurface can be calculated by the inversion process, although solutions to tomographic inversions are non-unique. Most commonly, only the travel time of the seismic waves is considered in the inversion. However, advances in modeling techniques and computing power have allowed different parts, or the entirety, of the measured seismic waveform to be fit during the inversion.<ref>{{Citation |last=Nolet |first=G. |chapter=Seismic wave propagation and seismic tomography |date=1987 |title=Seismic Tomography: With Applications in Global Seismology and Exploration Geophysics |pages=1–23 |editor-last=Nolet |editor-first=Guust |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-009-3899-1_1 |access-date=2024-09-15 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-3899-1_1 |isbn=978-94-009-3899-1|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Komatitsch |first1=Dimitri |title=The spectral-element method in seismology |date=2005 |work=Seismic Earth: Array Analysis of Broadband Seismograms, 2005 |pages=205–227 |url=https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/the-spectral-element-method-in-seismology |access-date=2024-09-15 |publisher=Blackwell Publishing Ltd. |last2=Tsuboi |first2=Seiji |last3=Tromp |first3=Jeroen|doi=10.1029/156GM13 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="doi.wiley.com">{{Cite journal |last1=Lawrence |first1=Jesse F. |last2=Prieto |first2=Germán A. |date=2011-06-15 |title=Attenuation tomography of the western United States from ambient seismic noise |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/2010JB007836 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |language=en |volume=116 |issue=B6 |doi=10.1029/2010JB007836 |bibcode=2011JGRB..116.6302L |issn=0148-0227|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Seismic tomography is similar to medical x-ray [[Computed Tomography|computed tomography]] (CT scan) in that a computer processes receiver data to produce a 3D image, although CT scans use [[attenuation]] instead of travel-time difference. Seismic tomography has to deal with the analysis of curved ray paths which are reflected and refracted within the Earth, and potential uncertainty in the location of the earthquake [[hypocenter]]. CT scans use linear x-rays and a known source.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.iris.edu/hq/inclass/downloads/optional/269|title=Seismic Tomography—Using earthquakes to image Earth's interior|publisher=IRIS Consortium|access-date=18 May 2016}}</ref>

== History ==
In the early 20th century, [[Seismology|seismologists]] first used travel time variations in seismic waves from earthquakes to make discoveries such as the existence of the [[Mohorovičić discontinuity|Moho]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mohorovičić |first1=A. |date=1910 |title=Potres od 8.x.1909; Das Beben vom 8.x.1909. |trans-title=The earthquake of 8 October 1909 |journal=Godisnje Izvjesce Zagrebackog Meteoroloskog Opservatorija za godinu 1909 – Jahrbuch des Meteorologischen Observatoriums in Zagreb für das Jahr 1909 [Yearbook of the Meteorological Observatory in Zagreb for the year 1909] |language=Croatian, German |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=1–63}}</ref> and the depth to the outer core.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gutenberg  |first=B. |date=1914 |title=Über Erdbebenwellen VIIA [About Earthquakes 7a]. |journal=Nachrichten von der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, Mathematisch-Physikalische Klasse. [News from the Society of Sciences in Göttingen, Mathematical-Physical Class]. |issue=1914 |pages=166–218}}</ref> While these findings shared some underlying principles with seismic tomography, modern tomography itself was not developed until the 1970s with the expansion of global seismic networks. Networks like the [[World-Wide Standardized Seismograph Network]] were initially motivated by [[Underground nuclear weapons testing|underground nuclear tests]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ammon |first1=C. J. |last2=Lay |first2=T. |last3=Simpson |first3=D. W. |date=2010-11-01 |title=Great Earthquakes and Global Seismic Networks |url=https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/srl/article/81/6/965-971/143758 |journal=Seismological Research Letters |language=en |volume=81 |issue=6 |pages=965–971 |doi=10.1785/gssrl.81.6.965 |bibcode=2010SeiRL..81..965A |issn=0895-0695|url-access=subscription }}</ref> but quickly showed the benefits of their accessible, standardized datasets for [[geoscience]]. These developments occurred concurrently with advancements in modeling techniques and computing power that were required to solve large [[inverse problem]]s<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Backus |first1=G. E. |last2=Gilbert |first2=J. F. |date=July 1967 |title=Numerical Applications of a Formalism for Geophysical Inverse Problems |journal=Geophysical Journal International |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1–3 |pages=247–276 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.1967.tb02159.x |doi-access=free |bibcode=1967GeoJ...13..247B |issn=0956-540X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Woodhouse |first=J. H. |date=1974-06-01 |title=Surface Waves in a Laterally Varying Layered Structure |journal=Geophysical Journal International |language=en |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=461–490 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.1974.tb04098.x |doi-access=free |bibcode=1974GeoJ...37..461W |issn=0956-540X}}</ref> and generate theoretical seismograms,<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=A Brief History of Seismology |url=https://earthquake.usgs.gov/hazards/about/workshops/thailand/downloads/CSMpp1_History.pdf |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160803190244/https://earthquake.usgs.gov/hazards/about/workshops/thailand/downloads/CSMpp1_History.pdf |archive-date=3 August 2016 |access-date=4 May 2016 |publisher=United States Geologic Survey (USGS)}}</ref> which are required to test the accuracy of a model.<ref name="Liu 31–662">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Q. |last2=Gu |first2=Y. J. |date=2012-09-16 |title=Seismic imaging: From classical to adjoint tomography |journal=Tectonophysics |volume=566–567 |pages=31–66 |bibcode=2012Tectp.566...31L |doi=10.1016/j.tecto.2012.07.006}}</ref> As early as 1972,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bois |first1=P. |last2=La Porte |first2=M. |last3=Lavergne |first3=M. |last4=Thomas |first4=G. |date=June 1972 |title=Well-To-Well Seismic Measurements |url=https://library.seg.org/doi/10.1190/1.1440273 |journal=Geophysics |language=en |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=471–480 |doi=10.1190/1.1440273 |bibcode=1972Geop...37..471B |issn=0016-8033|url-access=subscription }}</ref> researchers successfully used some of the underlying principles of modern seismic tomography to search for fast and slow areas in the subsurface.<ref name=":422">{{Cite journal |last1=Rawlinson |first1=N. |last2=Pozgay |first2=S. |last3=Fishwick |first3=S. |date=2010-02-01 |title=Seismic tomography: A window into deep Earth |journal=Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors |volume=178 |issue=3–4 |pages=101–135 |bibcode=2010PEPI..178..101R |doi=10.1016/j.pepi.2009.10.002|hdl=2381/27359 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The first widely cited publication that largely resembles modern seismic tomography was published in 1976 and used local earthquakes to determine the 3D velocity structure beneath Southern California.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aki |first1=Keiiti |last2=Lee |first2=W. H. K. |date=1976-08-10 |title=Determination of three-dimensional velocity anomalies under a seismic array using first P arrival times from local earthquakes: 1. A homogeneous initial model |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/JB081i023p04381 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |language=en |volume=81 |issue=23 |pages=4381–4399 |doi=10.1029/JB081i023p04381|bibcode=1976JGR....81.4381A |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":422" /> The following year, P wave delay times were used to create 2D velocity maps of the whole Earth at several depth ranges,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dziewonski |first1=Adam M. |last2=Hager |first2=Bradford H. |last3=O'Connell |first3=Richard J. |date=1977-01-10 |title=Large-scale heterogeneities in the lower mantle |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1029/JB082i002p00239 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |language=en |volume=82 |issue=2 |pages=239–255 |doi=10.1029/JB082i002p00239|bibcode=1977JGR....82..239D |url-access=subscription }}</ref> representing an early 3D model. The first model using iterative techniques, which improve upon an initial model in small steps and are required when there are a large number of unknowns, was done in 1984.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dziewonski |first=Adam M. |date=1984-07-10 |title=Mapping the lower mantle: Determination of lateral heterogeneity in P velocity up to degree and order 6 |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/JB089iB07p05929 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |language=en |volume=89 |issue=B7 |pages=5929–5952 |doi=10.1029/JB089iB07p05929 |bibcode=1984JGR....89.5929D |issn=0148-0227|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The model was made possible by iterating upon the first radially [[Anisotropy|anisotropic]] [[Preliminary reference Earth model|Earth model]], created in 1981.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dziewonski |first1=Adam M. |last2=Anderson |first2=Don L. |date=1981-06-01 |title=Preliminary reference Earth model |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0031920181900467 |journal=Physics of the Earth and Planetary Interiors |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=297–356 |doi=10.1016/0031-9201(81)90046-7 |bibcode=1981PEPI...25..297D |issn=0031-9201|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A radially anisotropic Earth model describes changes in material properties, specifically seismic velocity, along a radial path through the Earth, and assumes this profile is valid for every path from the core to the surface. This 1984 study was also the first to apply the term "tomography" to seismology, as the term had originated in the medical field with [[X-ray Tomography|X-ray tomography]].<ref name="Liu 31–662" />

Seismic tomography has continued to improve in the past several decades since its initial conception. The development of adjoint inversions, which are able to combine several different types of seismic data into a single inversion, help negate some of the trade-offs associated with any individual data type.<ref name="Liu 31–662" /> Historically, seismic waves have been modeled as 1D rays, a method referred to as "ray theory" that is relatively simple to model and can usually fit travel-time data well.<ref>{{Citation |last=Nolet |first=G. |chapter=Waveform tomography |date=1987 |title=Seismic Tomography: With Applications in Global Seismology and Exploration Geophysics |pages=301–322 |editor-last=Nolet |editor-first=Guust |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-009-3899-1_13 |access-date=2024-10-15 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-3899-1_13 |isbn=978-94-009-3899-1|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, recorded seismic waveforms contain much more information than just travel-time and are affected by a much [[Banana Doughnut theory|wider path]] than is assumed by ray theory. Methods like the finite-frequency method attempt to account for this within the framework of ray theory.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Montelli |first1=Raffaella |last2=Nolet |first2=Guust |last3=Dahlen |first3=F. A. |last4=Masters |first4=Guy |last5=Engdahl |first5=E. Robert |last6=Hung |first6=Shu-Huei |date=2004-01-16 |title=Finite-Frequency Tomography Reveals a Variety of Plumes in the Mantle |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1092485 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=303 |issue=5656 |pages=338–343 |doi=10.1126/science.1092485 |pmid=14657505 |bibcode=2004Sci...303..338M |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> More recently, the development of "full waveform" or "waveform" tomography has abandoned ray theory entirely. This method models seismic wave propagation in its full complexity and can yield more accurate images of the subsurface. Originally these inversions were developed in exploration seismology<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Igel |first1=Heinder |last2=Djikpéssé |first2=Hugues |last3=Tarantola |first3=Albert |date=February 1996 |title=Waveform inverstion of marine reflection seismograms for P impedance and Poisson's ratio |journal=Geophysical Journal International |language=en |volume=124 |issue=2 |pages=363–371 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.1996.tb07026.x|doi-access=free |bibcode=1996GeoJI.124..363I }}</ref> in the 1980s and 1990s and were too computationally complex for global and regional scale studies,<ref name="Liu 31–662" /> but development of numerical modeling methods to simulate seismic waves<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Komatitsch |first1=Dimitri |last2=Vilotte |first2=Jean-Pierre |date=1998-04-01 |title=The spectral element method: An efficient tool to simulate the seismic response of 2D and 3D geological structures |url=https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/bssa/article/88/2/368/120304/The-spectral-element-method-An-efficient-tool-to |journal=Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America |language=en |volume=88 |issue=2 |pages=368–392 |doi=10.1785/BSSA0880020368 |bibcode=1998BuSSA..88..368K |issn=1943-3573|url-access=subscription }}</ref> has allowed waveform tomography to become more common.

== Process ==
Seismic tomography uses seismic records to create 2D and 3D models of the subsurface through an [[inverse problem]] that minimizes the difference between the created model and the observed seismic data.<ref name=":422"/> Various methods are used to resolve anomalies in the [[Crust (geology)|crust]], [[lithosphere]], [[Mantle (geology)|mantle]], and [[Earth's core|core]] based on the availability of data and types of seismic waves that pass through the region. Longer wavelengths penetrate deeper into the Earth, but seismic waves are not sensitive to features significantly smaller than their wavelength and therefore provide a lower resolution. Different methods also make different assumptions, which can have a large effect on the image created. For example, commonly used tomographic methods work by iteratively improving an initial input model, and thus can produce unrealistic results if the initial model is unreasonable.<ref name=":422"/>

P wave data are used in most local models and global models in areas with sufficient earthquake and seismograph density. S and surface wave data are used in global models when this coverage is not sufficient, such as in ocean basins and away from [[subduction]] zones. First-arrival times are the most widely used, but models utilizing [[Seismic wave#Notation|reflected and refracted phases]] are used in more complex models, such as those imaging the core. Differential traveltimes between wave phases or types are also used.

=== Local tomography ===
Local tomographic models are often based on a temporary seismic array targeting specific areas, unless in a seismically active region with extensive permanent network coverage. These allow for the imaging of the crust and [[upper mantle (Earth)|upper mantle]].
* ''Diffraction and wave equation tomography'' use the full waveform, rather than just the first arrival times. The inversion of amplitude and phases of all arrivals provide more detailed density information than transmission traveltime alone. Despite the theoretical appeal, these methods are not widely employed because of the computing expense and difficult inversions.
* ''Reflection tomography'' originated with [[exploration geophysics]]. It uses an artificial source to resolve small-scale features at crustal depths.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brzostowski |first1=Matthew |last2=McMechan |first2=George |title=3-D tomographic imaging of near-surface seismic velocity and attenuation |url=https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/geophysics/article-abstract/57/3/396/72696/3-D-tomographic-imaging-of-near-surface-seismic |journal=Geophysics |publisher=Society of Exploration Geophysicists |access-date=2 June 2023 |date=1992|volume=57 |issue=3 |pages=396–403 |doi=10.1190/1.1443254 |bibcode=1992Geop...57..396B |url-access=subscription }}</ref> ''Wide-angle tomography'' is similar, but with a wide source to receiver offset. This allows for the detection of seismic waves refracted from sub-crustal depths and can determine continental architecture and details of plate margins. These two methods are often used together.
* ''Local earthquake tomography'' is used in seismically active regions with sufficient seismometer coverage. Given the proximity between source and receivers, a precise earthquake focus location must be known. This requires the simultaneous iteration of both structure and focus locations in model calculations.<ref name=":422"/>
* ''Teleseismic tomography'' uses waves from distant earthquakes that deflect upwards to a local seismic array. The models can reach depths similar to the array aperture, typically to depths for imaging the crust and lithosphere (a few hundred kilometers). The waves travel near 30° from vertical, creating a vertical distortion to compact features.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://www.mantleplumes.org/WebpagePDFs/Seismology.pdf|title=Seismology: The Hunt for Plumes|last=Julian|first=Bruce|date=2006|publisher=mantleplumes.org|access-date=3 May 2016}}</ref>

=== Regional or global tomography ===
[[File:FarallonTomoSlice.png|thumb|267x267px|Simplified and interpreted P and S wave velocity variations in the mantle across southern North America showing the subducted Farallon plate.]]
Regional to global scale tomographic models are generally based on long wavelengths. Various models have better agreement with each other than local models due to the large feature size they image, such as [[Subduction|subducted slabs]] and [[Large low-shear-velocity provinces|superplumes]]. The trade off from whole mantle to whole Earth coverage is the coarse resolution (hundreds of kilometers) and difficulty imaging small features (e.g. narrow plumes). Although often used to image different parts of the subsurface, P and S wave derived models broadly agree where there is image overlap. These models use data from both permanent seismic stations and supplementary temporary arrays.
* First arrival traveltime ''P wave'' data are used to generate the highest resolution tomographic images of the mantle. These models are limited to regions with sufficient seismograph coverage and earthquake density, therefore cannot be used for areas such as inactive plate interiors and ocean basins without seismic networks. Other phases of P waves are used to image the deeper mantle and core.
* In areas with limited [[seismograph]] or earthquake coverage, multiple phases of ''S waves'' can be used for tomographic models. These are of lower resolution than P wave models, due to the distances involved and fewer bounce-phase data available. S waves can also be used in conjunction with P waves for differential arrival time models.
* ''Surface waves'' can be used for tomography of the crust and upper mantle where no body wave (P and S) data are available. Both Rayleigh and Love waves can be used. The low frequency waves lead to low resolution models, therefore these models have difficulty with crustal structure. ''Free oscillations'', or [[normal mode]] [[seismology]], are the long wavelength, low frequency movements of the surface of the Earth which can be thought of as a type of surface wave. The frequencies of these oscillations can be obtained through [[Fourier transform]]ation of seismic data. The models based on this method are of broad scale, but have the advantage of relatively uniform data coverage as compared to data sourced directly from earthquakes.
* ''[[Attenuation]] tomography'' attempts to extract the [[Anelasticity|anelastic]] signal from the [[Elasticity (physics)|elastic]]-dominated waveform of seismic waves. Generally, it is assumed that seismic waves behave elastically, meaning individual rock particles that are displaced by the seismic wave eventually return to their original position. However, a comparatively small amount of permanent deformation does occur, which adds up to significant energy loss over large distances. This anelastic behavior is called [[attenuation]], and in certain conditions can become just as important as the elastic response. It has been shown that the contribution of anelasticity to seismic velocity is highly sensitive to temperature,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Yingjie |last2=Forsyth |first2=Donald W. |date=March 2008 |title=Attenuation in the upper mantle beneath Southern California: Physical state of the lithosphere and asthenosphere |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2007JB005118 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |language=en |volume=113 |issue=B3 |doi=10.1029/2007JB005118 |bibcode=2008JGRB..113.3308Y |issn=0148-0227|url-access=subscription }}</ref> so attenuation tomography can help determine if a velocity feature is caused by a thermal or chemical variation, which can be ambiguous when assuming a purely elastic response.<ref name="doi.wiley.com"/>
* ''Ambient noise tomography'' uses [[Seismic noise|random seismic waves]] generated by oceanic and atmospheric disturbances to recover the velocities of [[surface wave]]s. Assuming ambient seismic noise is equal in [[amplitude]] and [[frequency]] content from all directions, [[Cross-correlation|cross-correlating]] the ambient noise recorded at two seismometers for the same time period should produce only seismic energy that travels from one station to the other. This allows one station to be treated as a "virtual source" of surface waves sent to the other station, the "virtual receiver".<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last1=Bensen |first1=G.D. |last2=Ritzwoller |first2=M.H. |last3=Barmin |first3=M.P. |last4=Levshin |first4=A.L. |last5=Lin |first5=F. |last6=Moschetti |first6=M.P. |last7=Shapiro |first7=N.M. |last8=Yang |first8=Y. |date=June 1, 2007 |title=Processing seismic ambient noise data to obtain reliable broad-band surface wave dispersion measurements |journal=Geophysical Journal International |volume=169 |issue=3 |pages=1239–1260|doi=10.1111/j.1365-246X.2007.03374.x |doi-access=free |arxiv=2007.03374 |bibcode=2007GeoJI.169.1239B }}</ref> These surface waves are sensitive to the seismic velocity of the Earth at different depths depending on their [[Frequency|period]]. A major advantage of this method is that it does not require an earthquake or man-made source.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shapiro |first1=N. M. |date=11 March 2005 |title=High-Resolution Surface-Wave Tomography from Ambient Seismic Noise |journal=Science |volume=307 |issue=5715 |pages=1615–1618 |bibcode=2005Sci...307.1615S |doi=10.1126/science.1108339 |pmid=15761151 |s2cid=10846386}}</ref> A disadvantage of the method is that an individual cross-correlation can be quite noisy due to the complexity of the real ambient noise field. Thus, many individual correlations over a shorter time period, typically one day, need to be created and averaged to improve the [[signal-to-noise ratio]]. While this has often required very large amounts of seismic data recorded over multiple years,<ref name=":03" /> more recent studies have successfully used much shorter time periods to create tomographic images with ambient noise.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yadong |last2=Allam |first2=Amir |last3=Lin |first3=Fan-Chi |date=2019-11-28 |title=Imaging the Fault Damage Zone of the San Jacinto Fault Near Anza With Ambient Noise Tomography Using a Dense Nodal Array |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2019GL084835 |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |language=en |volume=46 |issue=22 |pages=12938–12948 |doi=10.1029/2019GL084835 |bibcode=2019GeoRL..4612938W |issn=0094-8276|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yadong |last2=Lin |first2=Fan-Chi |last3=Ward |first3=Kevin M |date=2019-02-27 |title=Ambient noise tomography across the Cascadia subduction zone using dense linear seismic arrays and double beamforming |url=https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/217/3/1668/5365997 |journal=Geophysical Journal International |volume=217 |issue=3 |pages=1668–1680 |doi=10.1093/gji/ggz109 |doi-access=free |issn=0956-540X}}</ref>
* [[Waveform]]s are usually modeled as [[Ray (optics)|rays]] due to ray theory being significantly less complex to model than the full seismic wave equations. However, seismic waves are affected by the material properties of a wide area surrounding the [[Banana Doughnut theory|ray path]], not just the material through which the ray passes directly. The [[Banana Doughnut theory|finite frequency effect]] is the result the surrounding medium has on a seismic record.<ref name=":9"/> ''Finite frequency tomography'' accounts for this in determining both travel time and amplitude anomalies, increasing [[image resolution]]. This has the ability to resolve much larger variations (i.e. 10–30%) in material properties.

== Applications ==
Seismic tomography can resolve anisotropy, anelasticity, density, and bulk sound velocity.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Romanowicz |first=Barbara |author-link=Barbara A. Romanowicz |date=2003-01-01 |title=GLOBAL MANTLE TOMOGRAPHY: Progress Status in the Past 10 Years |journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=303–328 |bibcode=2003AREPS..31..303R |doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.31.091602.113555}}</ref> Variations in these parameters may be a result of thermal or chemical differences, which are attributed to processes such as mantle plumes, subducting slabs, and mineral phase changes. Larger scale features that can be imaged with tomography include the high velocities beneath [[Shield (geology)|continental shields]] and low velocities under [[Mid-ocean ridge|ocean spreading centers]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last1=Kearey |first1=Philip |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JBF8UGc_M-sC&q=global%2520tectonics%2520kearey%2520and%2520vine&pg=PT9 |title=Global Tectonics |last2=Klepeis |first2=Keith A. |last3=Vine |first3=Frederick J. |date=2013-05-28 |publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] |isbn=978-1-118-68808-3 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Hotspots ===
[[File:Cartoon of African LLSVP.jpg|thumb|235x235px|The African large low-shear-velocity province (superplume)]]
The [[mantle plume]] hypothesis proposes that areas of volcanism not readily explained by [[plate tectonics]], called [[Hotspot (geology)|hotspots]], are a result of thermal upwelling within the mantle. Some researchers have proposed an upper mantle source above the [[Transition zone (Earth)|660km discontinuity]] for these plumes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Waite |first1=Gregory P. |last2=Smith |first2=Robert B. |last3=Allen |first3=Richard M. |date=April 2006 |title=V P and V S structure of the Yellowstone hot spot from teleseismic tomography: Evidence for an upper mantle plume |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2005JB003867 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |language=en |volume=111 |issue=B4 |doi=10.1029/2005JB003867 |issn=0148-0227}}</ref> while others propose a much deeper source, possibly at the [[Core–mantle boundary|core-mantle boundary]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pierce |first1=Kenneth L. |last2=Morgan |first2=Lisa A. |date=2009-11-20 |title=Is the track of the Yellowstone hotspot driven by a deep mantle plume? – Review of volcanism, faulting, and uplift in light of new data |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0377027309003023 |journal=Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research |volume=188 |issue=1 |pages=1–25 |doi=10.1016/j.jvolgeores.2009.07.009 |bibcode=2009JVGR..188....1P |issn=0377-0273|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

While the source of mantle plumes has been highly debated since they were first proposed in the 1970s,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Morgan |first=W. Jason |date=1972 |title=Deep Mantle Convection Plumes and Plate Motions |url=https://archives.datapages.com/data/bulletns/1971-73/data/pg/0056/0002/0200/0203.htm |journal=AAPG Bulletin |language=en-US |volume=56 |issue=2 |pages=203–213 |issn=0149-1423}}</ref> most modern studies argue in favor of mantle plumes originating at or near the core-mantle boundary.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Koppers |first1=Anthony A. P. |last2=Becker |first2=Thorsten W. |last3=Jackson |first3=Matthew G. |last4=Konrad |first4=Kevin |last5=Müller |first5=R. Dietmar |last6=Romanowicz |first6=Barbara |last7=Steinberger |first7=Bernhard |last8=Whittaker |first8=Joanne M. |date=2021-05-25 |title=Mantle plumes and their role in Earth processes |journal=Nature Reviews Earth & Environment |volume=2 |issue=6 |pages=382–401 |doi=10.1038/s43017-021-00168-6 |bibcode=2021NRvEE...2..382K |hdl=10852/90526 |issn=2662-138X|hdl-access=free }}</ref> This is in large part due to tomographic images that reveal both the plumes themselves<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montelli |first1=R. |last2=Nolet |first2=G. |last3=Dahlen |first3=F. A. |last4=Masters |first4=G. |date=November 2006 |title=A catalogue of deep mantle plumes: New results from finite-frequency tomography |journal=Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems |volume=7 |issue=11 |doi=10.1029/2006gc001248 |bibcode=2006GGG.....711007M |issn=1525-2027}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=French |first1=Scott W. |last2=Romanowicz |first2=Barbara |date=September 2015 |title=Broad plumes rooted at the base of the Earth's mantle beneath major hotspots |journal=Nature |volume=525 |issue=7567 |pages=95–99 |doi=10.1038/nature14876 |pmid=26333468 |bibcode=2015Natur.525...95F |issn=0028-0836}}</ref> as well as large low-velocity zones in the deep mantle that likely contribute to the formation of mantle plumes. These [[Large low-shear-velocity provinces|large low-shear velocity provinces]] as well as smaller [[Ultra-low velocity zone|ultra low velocity zones]] have been consistently observed across many tomographic models of the deep Earth<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McNamara |first=Allen K. |date=2019-06-05 |title=A review of large low shear velocity provinces and ultra low velocity zones |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0040195118301586 |journal=Tectonophysics |series=Linking Plate Tectonics and Volcanism to Deep Earth Dynamics – a tribute to Trond H. Torsvik |volume=760 |pages=199–220 |doi=10.1016/j.tecto.2018.04.015 |bibcode=2019Tectp.760..199M |issn=0040-1951|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Subduction Zones ===
[[Slab (geology)|Subducting plates]] are colder than the mantle into which they are moving. This creates a fast anomaly that is visible in tomographic images. Tomographic images have been made of most [[Subduction|subduction zones]] around the world and have provided insight into the geometries of the crust and upper mantle in these areas. These images have revealed that subducting plates vary widely in how steeply they move into the mantle.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Portner |first1=Daniel Evan |last2=Rodríguez |first2=Emily E. |last3=Beck |first3=Susan |last4=Zandt |first4=George |last5=Scire |first5=Alissa |last6=Rocha |first6=Marcelo P. |last7=Bianchi |first7=Marcelo B. |last8=Ruiz |first8=Mario |last9=França |first9=George Sand |last10=Condori |first10=Cristobal |last11=Alvarado |first11=Patricia |date=May 2020 |title=Detailed Structure of the Subducted Nazca Slab into the Lower Mantle Derived From Continent-Scale Teleseismic P Wave Tomography |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2019JB017884 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |language=en |volume=125 |issue=5 |doi=10.1029/2019JB017884 |bibcode=2020JGRB..12517884P |issn=2169-9313}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hall |first1=Robert |last2=Spakman |first2=Wim |date=2002-07-30 |title=Subducted slabs beneath the eastern Indonesia–Tonga region: insights from tomography |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0012821X02007057 |journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters |volume=201 |issue=2 |pages=321–336 |doi=10.1016/S0012-821X(02)00705-7 |bibcode=2002E&PSL.201..321H |issn=0012-821X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Tomographic images have also seen features such as deeper portions of the subducting plate [[Slab detachment|tearing off]] from the upper portion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schmandt |first1=Brandon |last2=Humphreys |first2=Eugene |date=2010-09-01 |title=Complex subduction and small-scale convection revealed by body-wave tomography of the western United States upper mantle |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0012821X1000422X |journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters |volume=297 |issue=3 |pages=435–445 |doi=10.1016/j.epsl.2010.06.047 |bibcode=2010E&PSL.297..435S |issn=0012-821X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Limitations ==
Global seismic networks have expanded steadily since the 1960s, but are still concentrated on continents and in seismically active regions. Oceans, particularly in the southern hemisphere, are under-covered.<ref name=":52">{{Cite web |last=Julian |first=Bruce |date=2006 |title=Seismology: The Hunt for Plumes |url=http://www.mantleplumes.org/WebpagePDFs/Seismology.pdf |access-date=3 May 2016 |publisher=mantleplumes.org}}</ref> Temporary seismic networks have helped improve tomographic models in regions of particular interest, but typically only collect data for months to a few years. The uneven distribution of earthquakes biases tomographic models towards seismically active regions. Methods that do not rely on earthquakes such as active source surveys or ambient noise tomography have helped image areas with little to no seismicity, though these both have their own limitations as compared to earthquake-based tomography.

The type of seismic wave used in a model limits the resolution it can achieve. Longer wavelengths are able to penetrate deeper into the Earth, but can only be used to resolve large features. Finer resolution can be achieved with surface waves, with the trade off that they cannot be used in models deeper than the crust and upper mantle. The disparity between wavelength and feature scale causes anomalies to appear of reduced magnitude and size in images. P and S wave models respond differently to the types of anomalies. Models based solely on the wave that arrives first naturally prefer faster pathways, causing models based on these data to have lower resolution of slow (often hot) features.<ref name=":422"/> This can prove to be a significant issue in areas such as volcanoes where rocks are much hotter than their surroundings and oftentimes partially melted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maguire |first1=Ross |last2=Schmandt |first2=Brandon |last3=Chen |first3=Min |last4=Jiang |first4=Chengxin |last5=Li |first5=Jiaqi |last6=Wilgus |first6=Justin |date=August 2022 |title=Resolving Continental Magma Reservoirs With 3D Surface Wave Tomography |journal=Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems |language=en |volume=23 |issue=8 |doi=10.1029/2022GC010446 |bibcode=2022GGG....2310446M |issn=1525-2027|doi-access=free }}</ref> Shallow models must also consider the significant lateral velocity variations in [[continental crust]].

Because seismometers have only been deployed in large numbers since the late-20th century, tomography is only capable of viewing changes in velocity structure over decades. For example, tectonic plates only move at millimeters per year, so the total amount of change in geologic structure due to plate tectonics since the development of seismic tomography is several orders of magnitude lower than the finest resolution possible with modern seismic networks.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dziewonski |first=Adam |title=Global Seismic Tomography: What we really can say and what we make up |url=http://www.mantleplumes.org/Penrose/PenPDFAbstracts/Dziewonski_Adam_abs.pdf |access-date=18 May 2016 |publisher=mantleplumes.org}}</ref> However, seismic tomography has still been used to view near-surface velocity structure changes at time scales of years to months.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Martini |first1=Francesca |last2=Bean |first2=Christopher J. |last3=Saccorotti |first3=Gilberto |last4=Viveiros |first4=Fatima |last5=Wallenstein |first5=Nicolau |date=April 2009 |title=Seasonal cycles of seismic velocity variations detected using coda wave interferometry at Fogo volcano, São Miguel, Azores, during 2003–2004 |journal=Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research |volume=181 |issue=3–4 |pages=231–246 |doi=10.1016/j.jvolgeores.2009.01.015 |bibcode=2009JVGR..181..231M |issn=0377-0273}}</ref><ref name=":13"/>

Tomographic solutions are non-unique. Although statistical methods can be used to analyze the validity of a model, unresolvable uncertainty remains.<ref name=":422"/> This contributes to difficulty comparing the validity of different model results.

Computing power limits the amount of seismic data, number of unknowns, mesh size, and iterations in tomographic models. This is of particular importance in ocean basins, which due to limited network coverage and earthquake density require more complex processing of distant data. Shallow oceanic models also require smaller model mesh size due to the thinner crust.<ref name="Liu 31–662"/>

Tomographic images are typically presented with a color ramp representing the strength of the anomalies. This has the consequence of making equal changes appear of differing magnitude based on visual perceptions of color, such as the change from orange to red being more subtle than blue to yellow. The degree of color saturation can also visually skew interpretations. These factors should be considered when analyzing images.<ref name=":1" />
